objective: By the end of this lesson you can plan and fly a commercial VFR trip through every class and type of airspace, including Class A limits, special use airspace, TFRs, SFRAs and special VFR, and state the weather, radio and equipment rules for each one at commercial standards.
why: Commercial flying puts you higher, faster and farther from home, often with a customer waiting. One missed boundary, TFR or equipment rule can end a job, a career, or a life, so you must know the airspace cold.

warmup: You are paid to fly a survey job 180 NM away. The direct line crosses an active MOA, passes 4 NM from a stadium on game day, and you want to cruise at 11,500 feet over mountains. Before you look anything up: which of those three things could legally stop you, and which only call for extra care?

key_terms.def: Generally 18,000 feet MSL up to and including FL 600. IFR only, with a clearance before entry. Not shown on VFR charts.
When two designations apply to the same airspace, the more restrictive rules apply: A, then B, C, D, E, and G last.
Surface to 10,000 feet MSL within 30 NM of the Part 91 Appendix D, section 1 airports. Altitude-reporting transponder and ADS-B Out required.
The two kinds of ADS-B Out. 1090ES works everywhere; UAT (978 MHz) is allowed only below 18,000 feet MSL, not in Class A.
An ATC clearance to fly in a surface area below basic VFR minimums: clear of clouds, at least 1 SM. Night only for an instrument-qualified pilot in an IFR-equipped airplane.
A restricted area that can be released to the FAA when not active, so ATC may route IFR traffic through it.
The list on the sectional border that gives each SUA area's altitudes, times of use and controlling agency. No NOTAM is issued for those listed times.
Temporary flight restriction issued by NOTAM under 14 CFR 91.137 to 91.145, for hazards, disasters, VIPs, space operations, air shows and sporting events.
Special air traffic rules in 14 CFR part 93. Some of those areas are designated Special Flight Rules Areas, like the Washington DC SFRA.
Low-altitude, high-speed military route. IR routes are flown IFR; VR routes need 5 miles visibility and a 3,000-foot ceiling.

chunks.title: How the airspace system is built

body.p: Airspace falls into two categories, regulatory and nonregulatory. Inside them are four types: controlled, uncontrolled, special use and other airspace [[33:175|AIM 3-1-1]].

bullets: Regulatory: Class A, B, C, D and E, plus restricted and prohibited areas [[33:175|AIM 3-1-1]].
Nonregulatory: MOAs, warning areas, alert areas, controlled firing areas and national security areas [[33:175|AIM 3-1-1]].
Controlled airspace means Class A, B, C, D and E. ATC service is given to IFR and VFR flights according to the class [[33:178|AIM 3-2-1]].
Class G is what is left: airspace not designated A, B, C, D or E [[33:189|AIM 3-3-1]].

body.p: The legal list of Class A to E areas is FAA Order JO 7400.11M, made part of 14 CFR part 71 by reference [[60:411|14 CFR 71.1]]. The rules for flying in each class are in part 91.

callout.text: Where two designations overlap, the more restrictive one's rules apply. Class A is most restrictive, then B, C, D, E, and G is least [[60:412|14 CFR 71.9]] [[33:175|AIM 3-1-3]].

body.p: What changes at the commercial level is not the rules but the trips. You fly faster airplanes, at higher altitudes, on longer routes, for pay. So you cross more airspace per flight, and the examiner expects you to apply the rules to a real trip, not just recite them.

check.q: Class C airspace sits over the Class D surface area of a secondary airport. Whose rules apply in the overlap?
check.a: Normally Class C, the more restrictive one [[60:412|14 CFR 71.9]]. ATC may procedurally exclude part of the overlap while the secondary tower is open, and then you talk to that tower [[33:183|AIM 3-2-4]].

chunks.title: Flying high: Class A and the airspace just below it

body.p: Class A is generally 18,000 feet MSL up to and including FL 600, including the airspace over waters within 12 NM of the coast of the 48 contiguous states and Alaska [[33:179|AIM 3-2-2]]. It is not drawn on VFR charts, but it is there [[2:16|Chart Users' Guide p.16]].

bullets: Flight rules: all operations are IFR, under a clearance received before you enter [[60:456|14 CFR 91.135(a)]].
Pilot: you may act as PIC under IFR only with an instrument rating for the aircraft category and class (or an ATP) [[60:191|14 CFR 61.3(e)]].
Radio: a two-way radio on the ATC frequency, and you must keep in contact the whole time [[60:456|14 CFR 91.135(b)]].
Transponder: Mode C altitude reporting [[60:494|14 CFR 91.215(b)(1)]].
ADS-B Out: the Class A rule lists only 1090ES equipment (TSO-C166b or C166c) [[60:498|14 CFR 91.225(a)]]. UAT (978 MHz) is allowed only below 18,000 feet [[33:301|AIM 4-5-7]].

Deviations: with an inoperative transponder, ATC may approve the flight right away to your destination or a repair shop. Other deviation requests must be in writing at least 4 days ahead [[60:456|14 CFR 91.135(d)]].

body.p: VFR tops out below Class A. Above 3,000 feet AGL and below 18,000 feet MSL, fly odd thousands plus 500 on magnetic courses 0 to 179, and even thousands plus 500 on 180 to 359 [[60:467|14 CFR 91.159(a)(1)]] [[60:468|14 CFR 91.159(a)(2)]]. So the highest VFR cruise is 17,500 eastbound and 16,500 westbound.

Below Class A, Class E normally starts at 14,500 feet MSL and goes up to, but not including, 18,000 feet. It does not include airspace less than 1,500 feet above the surface, unless designated lower [[33:187|AIM 3-2-6]] [[2:17|Chart Users' Guide p.17]]. Over very high terrain, Class G can reach above 14,500 MSL. Above FL 600 is Class E again [[33:187|AIM 3-2-6]].

callout.text: Speed: no more than 250 knots indicated below 10,000 feet MSL unless authorized [[60:448|14 CFR 91.117(a)]]. In a fast single descending from the flight levels, plan the slowdown before 10,000 feet.

check.q: Your turbocharged single is cruising VFR on a magnetic course of 075. What is the highest VFR cruising altitude you can use, and what stops you from going higher?
check.a: 17,500 feet MSL (odd thousand plus 500) [[60:467|14 CFR 91.159(a)(1)]]. At 18,000 feet MSL Class A begins, and all flight there must be IFR with a clearance [[60:456|14 CFR 91.135]].

callout.text: Your call sign opens the door. "N731CP, standby" means contact is made and you may enter C or D. "Aircraft calling, standby" or "remain outside" means stay out [[33:182|AIM 3-2-4]] [[33:186|AIM 3-2-5]].

bullets: Departing Class B VFR: you need a clearance. Tell clearance delivery your planned altitude and route [[33:181|AIM 3-2-3]].
ATC may give VFR aircraft in Class B altitudes that do not follow 91.159. When you hear "resume appropriate VFR altitudes," go back to a 91.159 altitude [[33:181|AIM 3-2-3]].
Departing a nontowered satellite airport inside C or D: call the controlling facility as soon as practicable after takeoff [[60:454|14 CFR 91.130(c)(2)(ii)]] [[60:453|14 CFR 91.129(c)(2)(ii)]].

Part-time airspace: some Class C areas give service only in published hours, and the radio and equipment rules then depend on the class set up outside those hours [[33:183|AIM 3-2-4]]. Part-time Class D becomes Class E or G; the Chart Supplement says which [[33:186|AIM 3-2-5]].
Radio failure under VFR in Class D: you may land if the weather is at or above basic VFR, you keep visual contact with the tower, and you get a clearance to land [[60:453|14 CFR 91.129(d)(2)]].
Large or turbine-powered airplanes enter a Class D traffic pattern at least 1,500 feet above the airport, unless cloud clearance requires lower [[60:453|14 CFR 91.129(e)(1)]].

check.q: You fly a fast single in the Class B surface area, 3 NM from the primary airport at 2,000 feet AGL. Is your speed limit 200 or 250 knots?
check.a: 250 knots. The 200-knot limit near a primary airport applies to Class C and D, and the rule says it does not apply inside Class B [[60:448|14 CFR 91.117(b)]]. ATC may still assign a speed.

chunks.title: Class E, Class G and towers outside Class D

body.p: Class E is controlled airspace that is not A, B, C or D. It has no specific pilot certificate or entry requirement, and ATC gives VFR aircraft no separation there [[33:187|AIM 3-2-6]] [[33:188|AIM 3-2-6]].

bullets: Surface areas: for an airport with no operating tower. The airport must have weather observation and reporting, and radio contact down to the runway [[33:187|AIM 3-2-6]].
Surface area extensions: Class E from the surface that holds instrument approaches without a radio requirement for VFR pilots [[33:188|AIM 3-2-6]].
Transition areas: Class E from 700 feet AGL (magenta vignette) or 1,200 feet AGL (blue vignette). They stay in effect all the time, whatever the airport hours [[33:188|AIM 3-2-6]].
Federal airways and low-altitude RNAV (T) routes: Class E from 1,200 feet AGL up to, but not including, 18,000 feet MSL, unless otherwise specified [[33:188|AIM 3-2-6]].
Offshore areas: Class E beyond 12 miles from the coast where ATC gives IFR en route service [[33:188|AIM 3-2-6]].

callout.text: A towered airport that has no Class D still needs radio contact. Establish it before 4 NM from the airport, up to and including 2,500 feet AGL [[60:452|14 CFR 91.126(d)]] [[60:452|14 CFR 91.127(c)]].
Flying exactly at the base of a Class E area counts as being in the airspace below it, for weather minimums [[60:466|14 CFR 91.155(e)]].

check.q: Your destination tower is closed and the Chart Supplement says "other times Class G." What is the airspace above the surface now?
check.a: Class G up to, but not including, the overlying controlled airspace, which is normally Class E starting at 700 or 1,200 feet AGL [[33:186|AIM 3-2-5]].

body.p: If your transponder works, it must be on with altitude reporting in all controlled airspace, replying on the code ATC gives you [[60:494|14 CFR 91.215(c)]]. ADS-B Out must transmit at all times unless ATC directs otherwise [[60:499|14 CFR 91.225(f)]]. VFR, the code is 1200 unless ATC assigns another [[33:222|AIM 4-1-20]].
If you have both, the Mode C and ADS-B Out altitude must come from the same source [[60:495|14 CFR 91.217(b)]].

callout.text: Deviations: Mode C not working, or a broken transponder or ADS-B Out going to your destination or a repair shop: ask ATC at any time. No transponder or no ADS-B Out installed: ask at least 1 hour before the flight [[60:494|14 CFR 91.215(d)(1)]] [[60:495|14 CFR 91.215(d)(2),(3)]] [[60:500|14 CFR 91.225(g)]]. The AIM says the ADS-B request goes through the FAA web tool, 1 to 24 hours before [[33:180|AIM 3-2-3]].

check.q: Your ADS-B Out fails on a trip. Home base is inside a Class C. What can you do?
check.a: Ask the ATC facility for an authorized deviation. For an inoperative ADS-B Out going to your destination or a repair shop, you may ask at any time [[60:500|14 CFR 91.225(g)(1)]].

chunks.title: Basic VFR weather minimums at commercial altitudes

body.p: No VFR flight with less flight visibility or cloud distance than the table shows for your class and altitude [[60:465|14 CFR 91.155(a)]]. Airplane rows only.

Flight visibility

Class G, 1,200 AGL or less (any MSL altitude), day
Class G, 1,200 AGL or less, night
Class G, above 1,200 AGL, below 10,000 MSL, day
Class G, above 1,200 AGL, below 10,000 MSL, night
Class G, above 1,200 AGL and at or above 10,000 MSL

callout.text: Crossing 10,000 MSL changes everything at once: visibility goes from 3 to 5 SM, below-cloud distance from 500 to 1,000 feet, and horizontal from 2,000 feet to 1 SM. Climbing over a layer? You need 1,000 feet above the tops either way.

bullets: Night pattern exception, Class G below 1,200 AGL: with 1 to 3 SM visibility, an airplane may fly clear of clouds in the traffic pattern within 1/2 mile of the runway [[60:466|14 CFR 91.155(b)(2)]].
Surface areas: no VFR beneath a ceiling of less than 1,000 feet, except special VFR [[60:466|14 CFR 91.155(c)]].
Surface areas of B, C, D or E: to take off, land or enter the pattern VFR you need 3 SM ground visibility, or 3 SM flight visibility if ground visibility is not reported [[60:466|14 CFR 91.155(d)]].

check.q: Class E at 10,500 feet MSL. Cloud bases are at 11,200 feet. Legal VFR?
check.a: No. At or above 10,000 MSL you need 1,000 feet below the clouds, so the bases must be at 11,500 or higher. You are only 700 feet below [[60:465|14 CFR 91.155(a)]].

body.p: Special VFR replaces 91.155 minimums with lower ones. It is allowed only below 10,000 feet MSL, inside the upward extension of a surface area of controlled airspace, and not at the airports in Part 91 Appendix D, section 3 [[60:467|14 CFR 91.157(a)]].

bullets: ATC clearance, clear of clouds, and at least 1 SM flight visibility [[60:467|14 CFR 91.157(b)(1)-(3)]].
Sunrise to sunset only, unless you meet the Part 61 requirements for instrument flight and the airplane is equipped for IFR under 91.205(d) [[60:467|14 CFR 91.157(b)(4)]].
Takeoff or landing: ground visibility at least 1 SM, or flight visibility 1 SM if ground visibility is not reported [[60:467|14 CFR 91.157(c)]].
At a Part 91 satellite airport with no weather reporting, flight visibility can be judged from the cockpit in takeoff position. That is not an official report [[60:467|14 CFR 91.157(c)(2),(d)]].

body.p: Ask the tower if there is one; in a Class E surface area, ask the nearest tower, FSS or center. The clearance has no set altitude, because you must stay clear of clouds, and you keep the job of terrain and obstacle clearance [[33:278|AIM 4-4-6]]. SVFR is given traffic permitting and when it will not delay IFR traffic [[33:277|AIM 4-4-6]].

callout.text: ATC separates SVFR flights from each other and from IFR flights, but only inside the surface area. Once you leave it, the clearance and the separation end [[33:278|AIM 4-4-6]]. Fixed-wing SVFR is banned at the Appendix D, section 3 airports, such as JFK, LaGuardia and Newark [[60:648|14 CFR Part 91 App. D]] [[60:649|14 CFR Part 91 App. D]], and the chart marks them "NO SVFR" [[2:17|Chart Users' Guide p.17]].

check.q: It is night. You are instrument rated and current, and your airplane is IFR equipped. The Class D reports 600 overcast and 2 SM. Can you ask for SVFR?
check.a: Yes. At night, airplane SVFR needs a pilot who meets the instrument requirements and an IFR-equipped airplane; you then fly clear of clouds with at least 1 SM [[60:467|14 CFR 91.157(b)]] [[33:278|AIM 4-4-6]].

bullets: Class B: solid blue lines. Ceiling over floor in solid blue, MSL, last two zeros dropped. A + before a floor means the floor is above that number; at or below it you are outside [[2:16|Chart Users' Guide p.16]].

Class C: solid magenta lines and numbers. A ceiling of "T" means up to, but not including, the Class B floor above. Magenta boxes give the approach frequency to call, generally within 20 NM [[2:16|Chart Users' Guide p.16]].
Class D: blue dashed line. Ceiling in a box; a minus sign means surface up to, but not including, that altitude [[2:16|Chart Users' Guide p.16]].

Class E surface area: magenta dashed line. Magenta vignette = Class E floor at 700 AGL. Blue vignette = other floors next to Class G. Other floors above 700 feet are marked with a number [[2:17|Chart Users' Guide p.17]].
Class E with a ceiling below 18,000 MSL: the word "ceiling" and the value along the edge [[2:17|Chart Users' Guide p.17]].
TRSA: screened black lines with black altitudes [[2:18|Chart Users' Guide p.18]].

callout.text: Some rules are not drawn. The 30 NM Mode C veil is a solid magenta circle, but the Mode C rule above Class C and the en route rule at and above 10,000 MSL (except at or below 2,500 AGL) are not depicted [[2:17|Chart Users' Guide p.17]]. Class A is not shown either [[2:16|Chart Users' Guide p.16]].

body.p: Part 93 airports have their names boxed, and "NO SVFR" above an airport name means no fixed-wing special VFR [[2:17|Chart Users' Guide p.17]]. Near Class B, use the Terminal Area Chart where its coverage is marked on the sectional; it has more detail [[2:20|Chart Users' Guide p.20]].

check.q: You plan 11,500 MSL across open country. The sectional shows no Mode C symbol there. Do you need a transponder?
check.a: Yes, unless you are at or below 2,500 feet AGL. The en route rule at and above 10,000 MSL applies but is not drawn on the chart [[2:17|Chart Users' Guide p.17]] [[60:494|14 CFR 91.215(b)(5)(i)]].

Unusual, often invisible hazards like artillery and missiles. Do not enter against its restrictions without permission of the using or controlling agency [[33:190|AIM 3-4-3]] [[60:456|14 CFR 91.133(a)]].
From 3 NM out from the coast; hazardous activity over domestic or international waters [[33:191|AIM 3-4-4]].
Separates military training from IFR traffic. VFR may enter, with extreme caution [[33:191|AIM 3-4-5]].

Not charted. Firing stops when an aircraft approaches [[33:191|AIM 3-4-7]].

bullets: Active MOA: military pilots may do aerobatics and are authorized above 250 knots below 10,000 MSL. Call any FSS within 100 miles for status, and the controlling agency for traffic advisories before you enter [[33:191|AIM 3-4-5]].
IFR through a MOA: ATC clears you through only if it can give IFR separation; otherwise it reroutes or restricts you [[33:191|AIM 3-4-5]].
IFR through a joint-use restricted area: if it is not active and released to the FAA, ATC lets you through with no special clearance. If it is active, ATC routes you around it [[33:190|AIM 3-4-3]].
Temporary MOAs and temporary restricted areas are not charted. Check NOTAMs and the FAA SUA website [[33:190|AIM 3-4-1]] [[33:191|AIM 3-4-5]].

body.p: On VFR charts, SUA is drawn only for the part below 18,000 MSL. Prohibited, restricted and warning areas are blue; MOAs and alert areas are magenta [[2:45|Chart Users' Guide p.45]]. Alert areas do not extend into Class A, B, C, D or Class E surface areas [[2:17|Chart Users' Guide p.17]].

callout.text: The SUA tabulation on the chart border lists altitudes, times of use and the controlling agency. No NOTAM is issued for the permanently listed times, so "no NOTAM" does not mean "not active" [[2:20|Chart Users' Guide p.20]]. Areas that need a NOTAM to activate are in the ARTCC NOTAMs [[33:192|AIM 3-4-9]].

check.q: A restricted area's chart listing says active 0700-2200 daily. You find no NOTAM. Is it active at 1500?
check.a: Plan on it. No NOTAM is issued for permanently listed times [[2:20|Chart Users' Guide p.20]]. Ask the controlling agency, whose frequency is in the chart margin [[33:192|AIM 3-4-9]], or stay out [[60:456|14 CFR 91.133(a)]].

body.p: The NOTAM starts with "FLIGHT RESTRICTIONS," then gives the location, times, area, altitudes, the FAA coordination facility and phone number, and the reason [[33:196|AIM 3-5-3]]. Air show and sporting event TFR NOTAMs come out at least 30 days ahead, unless the FAA has good cause [[60:461|14 CFR 91.145(f)]]. A NOTAM can also restrict flights when the pressure on your route goes above 31 inches of mercury [[60:459|14 CFR 91.144]].
ATC may approve flights into a TFR on its own only for 91.137(a)(2) and (a)(3) TFRs, and it will not approve local IFR flights into one [[33:196|AIM 3-5-3]].

callout.text: Commercial trap: a customer who pays you to look at or photograph a fire or flood does not fit the "to or from an airport" exception, because it excludes flights made to observe the disaster [[60:457|14 CFR 91.137(c)(4)]]. The (a)(3) rule says the same [[60:457|14 CFR 91.137(d)(1)]]. Carrying accredited news crews is its own exception: file a flight plan with the facility in the NOTAM first and, in an (a)(2) TFR, stay above the relief aircraft unless the on-scene official allows otherwise [[60:457|14 CFR 91.137(c)(5)]]. Only TFRs tied to national security are drawn on charts [[2:18|Chart Users' Guide p.18]].

check.q: Who may enter a 91.137(a)(1) TFR around a toxic gas leak?
check.a: Only aircraft taking part in the hazard relief work, under the direction of the official in charge on scene [[60:457|14 CFR 91.137(b)]].

chunks.title: SFRAs, special air traffic rules and other airspace areas

body.p: 14 CFR part 93 sets special air traffic rules (SATR) for certain areas. Some are designated Special Flight Rules Areas. Anyone flying to, from or within them must follow the part 93 rules unless ATC authorizes otherwise. SFRAs are drawn on sectionals, TACs and helicopter route charts [[33:202|AIM 3-5-7]].

The Washington DC SFRA is surface to, but not including, FL 180 within 30 miles of the DCA VOR/DME. It contains the DC Flight Restricted Zone (FRZ) [[60:705|14 CFR 93.335]]. To fly in it you need [[60:705|14 CFR 93.339(a)]]:

bullets: A working two-way radio, and contact with ATC before entry and the whole time inside.
A working altitude-reporting transponder squawking a discrete code from ATC. Never 1200 in the SFRA [[60:706|14 CFR 93.339(e)]].
For VFR, a DC SFRA or FRZ flight plan, activated when you get your code.
A Class B clearance for the Class B, and Class D rules in Class D.
Special Awareness Training to fly VFR within 60 NM of the DCA VOR/DME [[60:468|14 CFR 91.161(a)]].

callout.text: No part 91 or part 135 flight may operate in the DC FRZ unless that flight has an FAA/TSA authorization (with some exceptions such as approved security programs) [[60:706|14 CFR 93.341(a),(c)]]. Even an accidental SFRA violation can bring civil penalties and certificate action [[60:704|14 CFR 93.333]].

bullets: Military training routes: usually below 10,000 MSL at more than 250 knots. IR routes are flown IFR in any weather. VR routes need 5 miles visibility and no ceiling below 3,000 AGL [[33:193|AIM 3-5-2]] [[33:194|AIM 3-5-2]]. Four digits = no segment above 1,500 AGL; three digits = at least one above [[33:194|AIM 3-5-2]]. Routes can be several miles wide; call an FSS within 100 NM for activity [[33:195|AIM 3-5-2]].

Published VFR routes: a flyway is a general path to avoid Class B, no clearance [[33:198|AIM 3-5-5]]. A corridor is a hole through Class B, no clearance [[33:199|AIM 3-5-5]]. A transition route needs ATC contact, and a clearance for Class B [[33:199|AIM 3-5-5]].
TRSA: not a class of airspace. Extra radar service, voluntary for VFR [[33:201|AIM 3-5-6]].
Parachute jump areas: listed in the Chart Supplement [[33:197|AIM 3-5-4]].
Not charted: altitude reservations (ALTRV), announced by NOTAM, which VFR may fly through with vigilance, and ATC assigned airspace (ATCAA), with no NOTAM [[33:203|AIM 3-5-10]].
ADIZ: an area where ready identification and control of all aircraft is required for national security, shown with the ADIZ symbol [[2:18|Chart Users' Guide p.18]].

check.q: You want to use a charted VFR transition route over a Class B primary airport. When may you start it?
check.a: Only after ATC authorizes it. Talk to ATC and stay clear of Class B until you get the clearance [[33:199|AIM 3-5-5]].

chunks.title: Fly it step by step: the airspace plan for a commercial trip

bullets: 1. Draw the route on a current sectional, and on the TAC near busy terminal areas [[2:20|Chart Users' Guide p.20]]. List every airspace you fly in, under or over.

2. Pick altitudes: 91.159 cruising altitudes, a margin from Class B floors (mainly where the floor is 3,000 AGL or less), and terrain [[60:467|14 CFR 91.159]] [[33:181|AIM 3-2-3]] [[33:182|AIM 3-2-3]].
3. Match equipment to airspace: radio, Mode C, ADS-B Out (1090ES if you might go to Class A) [[60:494|14 CFR 91.215(b)]] [[60:499|14 CFR 91.225(d)]].
4. Check weather against 91.155 for each leg and each altitude band, and against surface area rules at both ends [[60:465|14 CFR 91.155]] [[60:466|14 CFR 91.155(c),(d)]].
5. Pull NOTAMs: TFRs, SUA activation, temporary SUA [[33:195|AIM 3-5-3]] [[33:192|AIM 3-4-9]]. Read SUA times in the chart tabulation [[2:20|Chart Users' Guide p.20]].
6. Write down frequencies: approach for Class C, towers, MOA controlling agencies, the FSS for MTR and MOA status [[2:16|Chart Users' Guide p.16]] [[33:191|AIM 3-4-5]].

7. In flight, call far enough out that you cannot enter C or D before contact, and get a Class B clearance before the line. Radar advisories do not change these duties [[33:182|AIM 3-2-4]] [[33:178|AIM 3-2-1]].
8. Keep an out: a turn, descent or diversion that keeps you legal if weather or ATC says no.

callout.text: If an ATC heading or altitude would take you into a cloud, over terrain too low, or into wake, tell ATC and get a new instruction. ATC service does not relieve you of VFR minimums or see and avoid [[33:181|AIM 3-2-3]] [[33:184|AIM 3-2-4]].

check.q: You are on flight following and approach has you in radar contact. You are 6 NM from a Class D you must cross. Who handles the tower call?
check.a: You do. The pilot must meet the Class B, C and D clearance or radio rules even while getting radar advisories [[33:178|AIM 3-2-1]].

body.p: Each kind of airspace brings its own hazard. Your job is to see it in planning, not discover it in flight.

bullets: Restricted areas: unusual, often invisible hazards. Going in without permission may be extremely hazardous [[33:190|AIM 3-4-3]].
MOAs and MTRs: fast, maneuvering military traffic, often low. Get status and advisories, or go around [[33:191|AIM 3-4-5]] [[33:195|AIM 3-5-2]].
Class B edges and floors: heavy traffic at the floor altitudes. Stay clear of the boundaries [[33:181|AIM 3-2-3]] [[33:182|AIM 3-2-3]].

TFRs: pop up on short notice, and only national security TFRs are on charts [[2:18|Chart Users' Guide p.18]]. In the DC SFRA, even an accidental violation can bring civil penalties and certificate action [[60:704|14 CFR 93.333]].
High altitude: higher minimums at and above 10,000 MSL, transponder and ADS-B rules, Class A above 18,000 [[60:465|14 CFR 91.155]] [[60:456|14 CFR 91.135]].
Below Class C shelves on approach, expect aircraft without transponders or ADS-B [[33:182|AIM 3-2-4]].

callout.text: External pressure is the commercial pilot's biggest airspace risk. A waiting customer or tight schedule pushes you to cut through an active area or squeeze under a low ceiling. Managing that pressure is the single most important key to risk management: plan for delays and accept them [[1:49|PHAK 2-10]].

check.q: Your customer is waiting, and going around an active restricted area adds 25 minutes. The direct line saves the time. What do you do?
check.a: Get permission from the controlling agency or go around and accept the delay. Entering without permission breaks 91.133 and exposes you to hidden hazards [[60:456|14 CFR 91.133(a)]] [[33:190|AIM 3-4-3]] [[1:49|PHAK 2-10]].

chunks.title: Reading the chart: SUA tables, Class E edges and security areas

body.p: Start with the tables on the chart border. Prohibited, restricted and warning areas are listed by number in blue. Alert areas are listed by number and MOAs by name, both in magenta. Each row gives the altitude, time of use, controlling agency and its frequency [[2:20|Chart Users' Guide p 20]].

Read the notes first. Altitudes are MSL unless the row says AGL, and times are local. TO means up to and including, so a row reading 4000 TO BUT NOT INCL 11,000 stops short of 11,000. NO A/G means no air-to-ground contact, so call the nearest FSS. For MOAs, the number is the floor, and a MOA reaches up to but not including FL 180 unless the row says otherwise. Alert areas do not extend into Class A, B, C or D airspace or Class E surface areas [[2:21|Chart Users' Guide p 21]]. No NOTAM is issued to announce permanently listed times of use [[2:20|Chart Users' Guide p 20]].

Now the edges of Class E. A magenta vignette is a Class E floor of 700 ft above the surface. A cyan (blue) vignette is a floor of 1,200 ft or more that meets Class G. A different floor is written as a number, such as 2400 AGL or 4500 MSL [[2:17|Chart Users' Guide p 17]].

Some limits are not on the chart. Only TFRs for national security are charted, shown with a broken blue line, so a clean chart does not mean a clear route. Read the NOTAMs for every other TFR. National security areas use a broken magenta line, and pilots should avoid flying through them [[2:18|Chart Users' Guide p 18]]. Enter a restricted or prohibited area only with permission of the using or controlling agency [[60:456|14 CFR 91.133(a)]].

check.q: Your chart shows no TFR along the route. Can you leave the NOTAM check out?
check.a: No. The chart shows only TFRs that relate to national security. A TFR for a disaster, special event or other hazard is a NOTAM and will not be on the chart [[2:18|Chart Users' Guide p 18]].

scenario.title: Positioning flight over the mountains
scenario.setup: You are a commercial pilot with an instrument rating. A company hires you to move its turbocharged single (Mode C transponder and UAT ADS-B Out) 260 NM west to a mountain airport, VFR. The route crosses terrain up to 9,000 feet MSL, passes a restricted area listed on the chart as active daily 0600-2000, and goes near a city where a NOTAM shows a VIP TFR today. The destination tower closes at 1800; the Chart Supplement says "other times Class E." You will arrive at 1830. The owner wants the airplane there tonight.

questions.q: You want to cruise high for terrain and winds. What altitudes can you use westbound VFR, and what equipment rules apply up there?
questions.a: Even thousands plus 500: up to 16,500 MSL [[60:468|14 CFR 91.159(a)(2)]]. At and above 10,000 MSL, more than 2,500 AGL, Mode C and ADS-B Out are required; you have both [[60:494|14 CFR 91.215(b)(5)(i)]] [[60:499|14 CFR 91.225(d)(4)]]. Your UAT is fine below 18,000 but not in Class A [[33:301|AIM 4-5-7]].

questions.q: At 14,500 MSL over terrain at 9,000 feet, what VFR minimums apply?
questions.a: You are 5,500 feet AGL and at the 14,500 MSL Class E floor. An airplane at the base of Class E counts as in the airspace below [[60:466|14 CFR 91.155(e)]], but either way the minimums are the same above 1,200 AGL and at or above 10,000 MSL: 5 SM visibility, 1,000 feet below, 1,000 above and 1 SM horizontal from clouds [[60:465|14 CFR 91.155(a)]] [[60:466|14 CFR 91.155(a)]].

questions.q: There is no NOTAM for the restricted area. May you fly through it at 1400?
questions.a: No, not without permission. No NOTAM is issued for permanently listed times, so treat it as active [[2:20|Chart Users' Guide p.20]]. Ask the controlling agency, or route around [[60:456|14 CFR 91.133(a)]] [[33:192|AIM 3-4-9]].

questions.q: How do you handle the VIP TFR?
questions.a: Read the full NOTAM for its area, altitudes and times, and plan to stay out unless the NOTAM allows your flight [[60:459|14 CFR 91.141]] [[33:196|AIM 3-5-3]]. These TFRs are usually not on the chart [[2:18|Chart Users' Guide p.18]].

questions.q: You arrive at 1830 with a reported 900-foot ceiling and 4 SM. What are your options?
questions.a: The surface area is now Class E [[33:186|AIM 3-2-5]]. With a ceiling under 1,000 feet you may not fly VFR beneath it in the surface area [[60:466|14 CFR 91.155(c)]]. You could ask the nearest tower, FSS or center for special VFR [[33:278|AIM 4-4-6]]; if it is after sunset, you must meet the instrument requirements and the airplane must be IFR equipped [[60:467|14 CFR 91.157(b)(4)]]. Or file IFR, or divert.

questions.q: The owner keeps calling to ask why you are not there yet. How do you manage that?
questions.a: Treat it as external pressure, the factor that can make you ignore all the others. Tell the owner your plan and a realistic time, and accept the delay [[1:49|PHAK 2-10]].

skills.do: For a planned commercial cross-country, state the basic VFR minimums for each class and altitude band on the route (including above 10,000 MSL and in surface areas), and decide from reports and forecasts whether each leg can be flown legally VFR or needs special VFR, IFR or a change of plan.
skills.practice: Write the 91.155 table from memory. Then pick a real high-altitude route and, for each leg, compare forecast clouds and visibility with the row that applies [[60:465|14 CFR 91.155(a)]] [[60:466|14 CFR 91.155(c),(d)]].

skills.do: Identify every airspace on the route from the sectional and TAC, give floors and ceilings, and state the clearance or radio contact and equipment (radio, Mode C, ADS-B Out type) each needs, including rules that are not drawn on the chart.
skills.practice: Trace a route past a Class B and over a Class C on a current chart. Label each boundary and say its entry and equipment rule [[2:16|Chart Users' Guide p.16]] [[2:17|Chart Users' Guide p.17]] [[60:494|14 CFR 91.215(b)]] [[60:499|14 CFR 91.225(d)]].

skills.do: Find all SUA and TFRs on or near the route, explain how to check their status and what is required to enter, and, if near a part 93 area or SFRA, state its rules and how you will comply or avoid it.
skills.practice: For your route, read each SUA entry in the chart tabulation and pull the NOTAMs [[2:20|Chart Users' Guide p.20]] [[33:192|AIM 3-4-9]]. Brief the DC SFRA rules to your instructor as a drill, and take the Special Awareness Training if you will fly near DC [[60:705|14 CFR 93.339]] [[60:468|14 CFR 91.161]].

quiz.q: What must you have before entering Class A airspace?
options: Permission from the nearest flight service station by radio
A written waiver from the nearest FAA flight standards office
A VFR flight plan on file and an operating transponder
An ATC clearance received before entering, under IFR
quiz.why: All Class A flight is IFR under a clearance received before entering the airspace [[60:456|14 CFR 91.135(a)]].

quiz.q: Approach says: "N731CP, radar contact, maintain VFR." You are 5 NM outside Class B. May you enter?
options: No, radar contact is not a Class B clearance
Yes, if you stay above the floor of the shelf
Yes, since radar contact counts as a clearance
No, VFR aircraft may never enter Class B airspace
quiz.why: Class B needs an ATC clearance before entry [[60:455|14 CFR 91.131(a)(1)]]. Radar contact or advisories do not replace it [[33:178|AIM 3-2-1]].

quiz.q: The Class D tower replies: "N731CP, standby." What does that mean for entry?
options: You must remain outside the Class D until the tower clears you in
Two-way communication is established, so you may enter
You must climb above the Class D ceiling before you continue inbound
You need a specific ATC clearance to enter the Class D surface area
quiz.why: When the controller uses your call sign, even with "standby," radio communication is established and you may enter [[33:186|AIM 3-2-5]].

quiz.q: You cruise in Class E at 12,500 feet MSL. What are the VFR minimums?
options: 3 SM; 500 below, 1,000 above, 2,000 horizontal
1 SM; clear of clouds, as in Class G at that altitude
5 SM; 1,000 below, 1,000 above, 1 SM horizontal
3 SM; clear of clouds, as in the lower Class E airspace
quiz.why: Class E at or above 10,000 MSL needs 5 SM and 1,000 below, 1,000 above, 1 SM horizontal [[60:465|14 CFR 91.155(a)]].

quiz.q: Which pilot may get a special VFR clearance in an airplane at night?
options: One meeting Part 61 instrument requirements, in an IFR-equipped airplane
Any commercial pilot, in any airplane
Any pilot, if ground visibility is at least 3 SM
Any pilot who files a VFR flight plan first
quiz.why: Airplane SVFR between sunset and sunrise needs a pilot who meets the instrument flight requirements of Part 61 and an airplane equipped under 91.205(d) [[60:467|14 CFR 91.157(b)(4)]].

quiz.q: Which airspace requires ADS-B Out but not a transponder?
options: Class C airspace, from the surface up to the published ceiling
Within the 30 NM Mode C veil of a Class B primary airport
Class E at or above 3,000 MSL over the Gulf within 12 NM of the coast
Class B airspace above its published ceiling, up to 10,000 MSL, outside the veil
quiz.why: 91.225 adds the Gulf airspace for ADS-B Out, but 91.215 does not include it for transponders [[60:499|14 CFR 91.225(d)(5)]] [[33:187|AIM 3-2-6]].

quiz.q: Inside an active MOA, what may military pilots do that you might not expect?
options: Fly with their transponders off in Class B
Enter restricted areas without permission
Ignore VFR weather minimums near airports
Fly faster than 250 knots below 10,000 MSL
quiz.why: DoD is authorized above 250 knots below 10,000 MSL in active MOAs, and military pilots there are exempt from the aerobatic limits [[33:191|AIM 3-4-5]].

quiz.q: What is the normal size of a major sporting event TFR?
options: 5 NM radius, up to 17,000 feet MSL over the event
30 NM radius, up to 18,000 feet MSL over the event
3 NM radius, up to 2,500 feet above the surface
1 NM radius, up to 1,000 feet AGL over the stadium
quiz.why: A major sporting event TFR is normally 3 NM and 2,500 feet above the surface. 5 NM and 17,000 MSL is the normal air show size [[60:461|14 CFR 91.145(e)]].

quiz.q: Where on the sectional do you find a restricted area's altitudes, times of use and controlling agency?
options: Only in the Chart Supplement
Only in the ARTCC NOTAMs
In the boxed note at the nearest Class C
In the special use airspace tabulation on the chart border
quiz.why: The chart tabulation lists each SUA area with altitude, time of use and controlling agency or contact facility [[2:20|Chart Users' Guide p.20]] [[33:190|AIM 3-4-1]].

quiz.q: A part 135 charter wants to land at an airport inside the DC FRZ. What is required?
options: Only a DC SFRA flight plan on file
An FAA/TSA authorization for the flight
Only the Special Awareness Training course
Nothing beyond a Class B clearance
quiz.why: No part 91 or part 135 operation may be conducted in the DC FRZ unless the flight operates under an FAA/TSA authorization [[60:706|14 CFR 93.341(a)]].

quiz.q: In the tabulation, A-220 shows NO A/G in the agency column. What does that tell you?
options: You need an ATC clearance and a transponder before entering
The area has no published altitude limit above 1,500 ft AGL
No air-to-ground communication; contact the nearest FSS
The area is closed to all aircraft except military traffic
quiz.why: The notes define NO A/G as no air to ground communications and say to contact the nearest FSS [[2:21|Chart Users' Guide p 21]].

quiz.q: R-6602 B is listed as 4000 TO BUT NOT INCL 11,000. At which altitude is a pilot flying in R-6602 B?
options: 11,000 ft MSL
11,500 ft MSL
10,500 ft MSL
3,500 ft MSL
quiz.why: The area runs from 4,000 ft up to but not including 11,000 ft MSL. 11,000 is the floor of R-6602 C [[2:21|Chart Users' Guide p 21]].

quiz.q: Buckeye MOA is listed with an altitude of 5000. What does 5000 mean?
options: It is the floor; the MOA goes up to but not including FL 180
It is active from the surface until 5,000 ft AGL each day
Its ceiling is 5,000 ft MSL, with the floor at the surface
The MOA is about 5,000 ft wide at its widest point on the chart
quiz.why: The note says altitudes in the MOA table indicate the floor, and all MOAs extend to but do not include FL 180 unless otherwise noted [[2:21|Chart Users' Guide p 21]].

quiz.q: A magenta vignette runs along the edge of Class E airspace. What does it mark?
options: A Class E floor 700 ft above the surface
A Class E floor of 1,200 ft or more AGL
Class E airspace that starts at the surface
A shelf of Class B airspace over the area
quiz.why: Magenta vignettes define Class E floors of 700 ft above the ground; blue vignettes mark higher floors that abut Class G [[2:17|Chart Users' Guide p 17]].

quiz.q: Your sectional shows no TFR on your route. What does that prove?
options: Only that no MOA is active along your planned route
That TFRs do not exist at your planned cruise altitude
The route is clear of every TFR for the whole flight
Nothing. Charted TFRs are limited, so check NOTAMs
quiz.why: The chart shows only TFRs relating to national security. The actual NOTAM text holds the details [[2:18|Chart Users' Guide p 18]].

quiz.q: You cruise at 11,500 ft MSL in Class E airspace. What flight visibility and distance from clouds does VFR require?
options: 3 SM; 500 ft below, 1,000 ft above, 2,000 ft horizontal
5 SM; 1,000 ft below, 1,000 ft above, 1 SM horizontal
5 SM; 500 ft below, 1,000 ft above, 2,000 ft horizontal
3 SM; 1,000 ft below, 1,000 ft above, 1 SM horizontal
quiz.why: At or above 10,000 ft MSL in Class E: 5 SM, 1,000 ft below, 1,000 ft above and 1 SM horizontal [[60:465|14 CFR 91.155(a)]].

takeaways: Class A (18,000 MSL to FL 600) is IFR only: clearance, radio, Mode C and 1090ES ADS-B Out. Highest VFR cruise is 17,500 east, 16,500 west.
B needs a clearance; C and D need two-way contact with your call sign. Radar advisories never replace either.
At and above 10,000 MSL: 5 SM and 1,000/1,000/1 SM, plus Mode C and ADS-B Out unless at or below 2,500 AGL.
Special VFR: clearance, clear of clouds, 1 SM, surface areas only, never at NO SVFR airports; at night only if instrument qualified and IFR equipped.
No NOTAM does not mean an SUA area is inactive. Read the tabulation and ask the controlling agency.
Read every TFR NOTAM. A flight made to look at a disaster does not fit the airport exception; accredited news crews have their own rule.
Plan for delays: external pressure from customers is the risk that makes pilots break airspace rules.
cfi_notes: Part 91 Appendix D, section 2 (the 10 NM transponder airports in 91.215(b)(5)(ii)) is currently reserved, so no airports are listed. Older study guides that name such airports are out of date [[60:648|14 CFR Part 91 App. D]].

AIM TBL 3-1-2 still shows VFR flight levels from FL 185 to FL 290 [[33:177|AIM TBL 3-1-2]]. In the U.S. that airspace is Class A, which is IFR only, and 91.159(b) says to hold the ATC-assigned level above 18,000 [[60:468|14 CFR 91.159(b)]]. Examiners like this trap.
Many students think 14,500 MSL Class E applies everywhere. It excludes airspace less than 1,500 AGL, so over high peaks Class G goes higher [[33:187|AIM 3-2-6]].
Students often apply the 200-knot rule inside Class B. 91.117(b) says it does not apply there; 250 knots below 10,000 MSL does [[60:448|14 CFR 91.117]].

The CFR says ADS-B deviation requests for unequipped aircraft need 1 hour notice; the AIM adds that they go through a web tool, 1 to 24 hours before [[60:500|14 CFR 91.225(g)(2)]] [[33:180|AIM 3-2-3]]. Teach both.

AIM 4-4-6g says night fixed-wing SVFR needs an instrument-rated pilot. The rule, 14 CFR 91.157(b)(4), is stricter: the pilot must meet the Part 61 requirements for instrument flight, so currency counts [[33:278|AIM 4-4-6]] [[60:467|14 CFR 91.157(b)(4)]]. Teach the CFR.
Commercial students who fly UAT-equipped trainers should know UAT is not legal for Class A [[33:301|AIM 4-5-7]].
Use real sectionals and the chart tabulation for the S2 and S3 drills. Have the student brief SUA status and TFRs as they would to a customer.
gaps: Part 135 and operator-specific weather or airspace limits (operations specifications) are not in these sources and are not taught here.
ADIZ entry rules, DVFR flight plans (14 CFR part 99) and intercept procedures are only mentioned; they are not in the uploaded part 91 and AIM chapter 3 pages used here.
Standard sizes of VIP and national-security TFRs are set in each NOTAM, not in these sources.
Rules for part 93 areas other than the DC SFRA (for example the Grand Canyon or Los Angeles SFRAs) are not taught.
A current local sectional, TAC and Chart Supplement are needed for the chart drills; they are not among the resources.

activities.title: True or false: transponder and ADS-B
activities.intro: Decide if each statement is true or false.

cards.s: Installed ADS-B Out must transmit at all times unless ATC directs otherwise.
cards.why: True. ADS-B Out must be in transmit mode at all times, with narrow exceptions [[60:499|14 CFR 91.225(f)]].

cards.s: UAT (978 MHz) ADS-B Out meets the rule for Class A airspace.
cards.why: False. Class A needs 1090ES; UAT is only for below 18,000 feet [[60:498|14 CFR 91.225(a)]] [[33:301|AIM 4-5-7]].

cards.s: At 11,000 MSL, 1,800 feet above a ridge, the en route transponder rule applies.
cards.why: False. The at-and-above-10,000 rule excludes airspace at and below 2,500 feet AGL [[60:494|14 CFR 91.215(b)(5)(i)]].

cards.s: Above the ceiling of a Class C, inside its lateral limits, you need ADS-B Out up to 10,000 MSL.
With no transponder installed, you can ask for a Class C deviation from the runup area.
cards.why: False. For an aircraft not equipped with a transponder, the request must be made at least 1 hour before [[60:495|14 CFR 91.215(d)(3)]].

cards.s: VFR pilots squawk 1200 unless ATC assigns another code.
cards.why: True [[33:222|AIM 4-1-20]]. The exception is the DC SFRA, where 1200 is never allowed [[60:706|14 CFR 93.339(e)]].

items.q: You fly VFR on a magnetic course of 090. What is the highest VFR cruising altitude you may use, in feet MSL?
items.why: Courses 0 to 179 use odd thousands plus 500 below 18,000 MSL: 17,500. 18,000 is Class A, IFR only [[60:467|14 CFR 91.159(a)(1)]] [[60:456|14 CFR 91.135]].

items.q: A Class C primary airport is at 1,350 feet MSL. Its Class C goes to the standard 4,000 feet above the airport. What is the ceiling in feet MSL?
items.why: 1,350 + 4,000 = 5,350 feet MSL. Class C usually goes to 4,000 feet above airport elevation, charted in MSL [[33:182|AIM 3-2-4]].

items.q: A stadium sits at 650 feet MSL. Its sporting event TFR has the normal size. What is the top of the TFR in feet MSL?
items.why: Normal sporting event TFR: 2,500 feet above the surface. 650 + 2,500 = 3,150 MSL. Always confirm in the NOTAM [[60:461|14 CFR 91.145(e)(2)]].

items.q: You cruise at 11,500 feet MSL over terrain at 8,800 feet MSL. How many feet above the ground are you?
items.why: 11,500 - 8,800 = 2,700 feet AGL. That is more than 2,500 AGL, so the en route Mode C and ADS-B Out rules apply [[60:494|14 CFR 91.215(b)(5)(i)]] [[60:499|14 CFR 91.225(d)(4)]].

items.q: Cloud tops are at 9,800 feet MSL. You want to cruise VFR above them in Class E, at or above 10,000 MSL. What is the lowest altitude, in feet MSL, that meets the VFR cloud clearance rule?
items.why: At or above 10,000 MSL you need 1,000 feet above clouds: 9,800 + 1,000 = 10,800 MSL [[60:465|14 CFR 91.155(a)]].

activities.title: Survey flight decisions
activities.intro: You are flying N731CP, an IFR-equipped Cessna 182 with Mode C and ADS-B Out, on a paid aerial survey job. You hold a commercial certificate and an instrument rating and are current. The route crosses a MOA and passes south of a Class C, ending at a towered Class D airport.

steps.s: Preflight. The chart tabulation lists the MOA as active 0800-1700. You find no NOTAM for it. It is 1000.
options: Assume it is inactive because no NOTAM was issued for it
Plan to get MOA status from an FSS within 100 miles and have a route around it
Plan to cross it fast at 250 knots to limit your exposure
Cancel the job and fly the long way around, since VFR aircraft may not enter a MOA while it is active
steps.why: No NOTAM is issued for listed times [[2:20|Chart Users' Guide p.20]]. Get real-time status from any FSS within 100 miles [[33:191|AIM 3-4-5]].

steps.s: 15 NM from the MOA, the FSS says it is active with fighters from 5,000 to 15,000 MSL. You are at 7,500.
options: Continue straight through and keep looking
Squawk 7700 so the military sees you
Contact the controlling agency for traffic advisories before entering, or go around
Descend to 500 AGL and fly under the jets
steps.why: VFR may enter an active MOA with extreme caution, but you should contact the controlling agency for traffic advisories first [[33:191|AIM 3-4-5]].

steps.s: Past the MOA, 15 NM from the Class C, you call approach and hear: "Aircraft calling approach, standby."
options: Enter if you are below 2,500 AGL, since you called
Enter, since approach answered your call on the radio
Remain outside the Class C until approach calls you by call sign
Squawk 1200 and enter the Class C once approach has replied, then call again on the tower frequency
steps.why: Without your call sign, two-way communication is not established, and you may not enter [[33:182|AIM 3-2-4]].

steps.s: Near the destination, the ATIS reports 800 overcast and 3 SM. Sunset was 20 minutes ago.
options: Land VFR, because the visibility is 3 SM and that is enough
Fly in VFR at 500 feet below the cloud layer
Enter the surface area first, then call the tower for a clearance
Request special VFR from the tower and stay clear of clouds
steps.why: No VFR under a ceiling below 1,000 feet in the surface area [[60:466|14 CFR 91.155(c)]]. You are instrument current in an IFR-equipped airplane, so night SVFR is allowed with a clearance [[60:467|14 CFR 91.157(b)]].

steps.s: Cleared special VFR, you find lower clouds ahead. Staying clear of them would put you too close to a tower on the chart.
options: Tell the tower and ask for a new plan, such as an IFR clearance
Climb into the clouds for a moment and then descend
Leave the surface area to find better weather elsewhere
Press on just under the clouds with the tower in sight
steps.why: On SVFR you must stay clear of clouds, and you are still responsible for obstacle clearance [[33:278|AIM 4-4-6]]. Tell ATC and get a revised plan [[33:184|AIM 3-2-4]].

final_quiz.q: By day you fly 15,000 MSL over a ridge at 14,200 MSL. The chart shows no lower Class E there. Which VFR minimums apply?
options: 1 SM; clear of clouds
3 SM; 500 below, 1,000 above, 2,000 horizontal
5 SM; 1,000 below, 1,000 above, 1 SM horizontal
Not applicable; this is Class A
final_quiz.why: The 14,500 MSL Class E excludes airspace less than 1,500 AGL [[33:187|AIM 3-2-6]]. At 800 AGL you are in Class G at 1,200 AGL or less, regardless of MSL altitude: 1 SM and clear of clouds by day [[60:465|14 CFR 91.155(a)]].

final_quiz.q: A Class C airport is at 1,300 MSL with the standard 4,000-foot ceiling. You overfly it at 6,500 MSL. What equipment do you need?
options: Only ADS-B Out
Only a two-way radio
Nothing, because you are above Class C
Mode C transponder and ADS-B Out
final_quiz.why: Ceiling is 5,300 MSL. Above the ceiling and inside the lateral limits of Class C up to 10,000 MSL, both are required [[60:494|14 CFR 91.215(b)(4)]] [[60:499|14 CFR 91.225(d)(3)]].

final_quiz.q: Eastbound at 9,500, you want to climb above a layer with tops at 10,800 and cruise at 11,500 in Class E. Legal?
options: Yes, 500 feet above the cloud tops is enough at that altitude
No, you need 1,000 feet above the tops at that altitude
Yes, staying clear of clouds is all that is needed above 10,000 MSL
No, VFR on top above a layer is never allowed in Class E
final_quiz.why: 11,500 is 700 feet above the tops. At or above 10,000 MSL you need 1,000 feet above clouds [[60:465|14 CFR 91.155(a)]].

final_quiz.q: You want SVFR out of a Part 91 satellite airport with no weather reporting. How can visibility be determined?
options: Flight visibility from the cockpit in takeoff position may be used
The tower must estimate it for you
SVFR is not allowed without weather reporting
It must come from an official weather report
final_quiz.why: For Part 91 at a satellite airport without weather reporting, flight visibility includes what you see from the cockpit in takeoff position. It is not an official report [[60:467|14 CFR 91.157(c)(2),(d)]].

final_quiz.q: It is night. You are instrument rated but have not met the instrument currency rules. The airplane is IFR equipped. Can you get airplane SVFR?
options: Yes, the instrument rating alone is enough for night airplane SVFR
No, you must meet the Part 61 requirements for instrument flight
Yes, if the ground visibility is at least 3 SM at the airport
No, special VFR is never allowed in an airplane at night
final_quiz.why: At night the pilot must meet the applicable Part 61 requirements for instrument flight, and the airplane must be IFR equipped [[60:467|14 CFR 91.157(b)(4)]].

final_quiz.q: On an IFR flight plan, your route crosses a joint-use restricted area that is not active and has been released to the FAA. What happens?
options: ATC lets you through without a specific clearance for it
You must call the using agency yourself before you cross it
ATC must reroute you around it for the whole flight
You must cancel your IFR flight plan before you can cross it
final_quiz.why: When a joint-use restricted area is not active and has been released to the FAA, ATC allows IFR aircraft through without a specific clearance [[33:190|AIM 3-4-3]].

final_quiz.q: A TV station hires you to carry its accredited news crew over a wildfire inside a 91.137(a)(2) TFR. What is required?
options: Nothing, news flights are always allowed
A flight plan filed with the facility in the NOTAM, flying above relief aircraft
Only a squawk of 1255
Only permission from the nearest tower
final_quiz.why: Accredited news representatives may enter if a flight plan is filed first with the facility named in the NOTAM and the flight stays above relief aircraft altitudes, unless the on-scene official allows otherwise [[60:457|14 CFR 91.137(c)(5)]].

final_quiz.q: An air show TFR has the normal size. You plan to pass 3 NM from show center at 12,500 MSL. Problem?
options: No, air show TFRs end at 2,500 AGL like other event TFRs
No, only the show box itself is restricted, not the outer ring
No, unless you are below 10,000 MSL where the TFR applies
Yes, it normally covers 5 NM up to 17,000 MSL
final_quiz.why: An aerial demonstration TFR is normally a 5 NM radius up to 17,000 MSL, so 12,500 MSL at 3 NM is inside [[60:461|14 CFR 91.145(e)(1)]].

final_quiz.q: In flight, you want to know if a VR route ahead is in use. Who do you call?
options: The nearest control tower to the route
Any Class C approach control nearby
An FSS within 100 NM of the route
The military base, on 121.5
final_quiz.why: Contact the FSS within 100 NM of the MTR for times, altitudes and route width [[33:195|AIM 3-5-2]].

final_quiz.q: You will depart VFR from a Class B primary airport. What must you do?
options: Get a clearance and tell clearance delivery your altitude and route
Just call the tower for takeoff
File an IFR flight plan
Climb above 10,000 MSL before turning
final_quiz.why: Departing aircraft need a clearance to depart Class B and should give clearance delivery their altitude and route [[33:181|AIM 3-2-3]].

final_quiz.q: A Class C gives service only during published hours. After hours, what sets your radio and equipment requirements?
options: The Class C rules, which never change at any hour
Whatever the nearest approach control tells you to do
The class of airspace set up outside those hours
There are no requirements at all after published hours
final_quiz.why: Outside published hours, the communication and transponder/ADS-B requirements depend on the class of airspace established for those times [[33:183|AIM 3-2-4]].

final_quiz.q: You fly through a Class D surface area at 1,800 AGL, 3 NM from the primary airport. What is the maximum indicated airspeed unless ATC says otherwise?
options: 250 knots
200 knots
156 knots
230 knots
final_quiz.why: At or below 2,500 AGL within 4 NM of a Class C or D primary airport: 200 knots (230 mph) [[60:448|14 CFR 91.117(b)]].

final_quiz.q: Behind schedule with a customer waiting, you see the direct route crosses an active restricted area. Which is the best plan?
options: Cross it low and fast to save time
Cross it if no NOTAM was issued
Get permission from the controlling agency or route around and accept the delay
Cross it while talking to flight following
final_quiz.why: No flight in an active restricted area without permission of the using or controlling agency [[60:456|14 CFR 91.133(a)]]. Managing external pressure means accepting delays [[1:49|PHAK 2-10]].

final_quiz.q: A-220 is charted next to a Class D airport. Does the alert area reach into the Class D airspace?
options: Yes, all the way down to the surface of the Class D airport
Yes, but only at night while the airport beacon is operating
Yes, but only above 4,000 ft AGL near the Class D ceiling
No, alert areas do not extend into Class A, B, C or D airspace
final_quiz.why: The note under the alert area table says alert areas do not extend into those airspace areas [[2:21|Chart Users' Guide p 21]].

final_quiz.q: A military training route is numbered VR1007. What does the number tell you?
options: It has a segment above 1,500 ft AGL and is flown mainly IFR
No segment is above 1,500 ft AGL; it is flown mainly VFR
The route is 1,007 NM long, counted from the entry point
It is a route for helicopters and slow-flying aircraft only
final_quiz.why: Four-digit routes have no segment above 1,500 ft and are generally flown VFR. Routes with a segment above 1,500 ft AGL have three or fewer digits, such as IR21, and are flown IFR when possible [[2:18|Chart Users' Guide p 18]].

final_quiz.q: You fly at 11,000 ft MSL over terrain at 3,000 ft MSL, outside Class B and C airspace. Your airplane has an engine-driven electrical system. What equipment is required?
options: A VOR receiver and DME for en route navigation
Nothing extra, since you are in Class E airspace
A transponder with Mode C altitude reporting
A two-way radio and a VOR receiver, no transponder
final_quiz.why: At and above 10,000 ft MSL in the 48 states, excluding airspace at and below 2,500 ft AGL, you need a transponder with altitude reporting [[60:494|14 CFR 91.215(b)(5)(i)]]. Here you are 8,000 ft AGL.
